title: Security review - status page + incident communications (Northbridge AI Platform)
summary: Northbridge asked detailed questions about Redwood's incident process and customer-facing communications: how incidents are declared (severity + criteria), how the public status page is updated and approved during Sev0/Sev1, what information is included/excluded in post-incident summaries, and how Dedicated/Private deployments are handled without leaking customer-specific capacity or topology. Redwood shared the current roles (Incident Commander, Comms Lead, Scribe), target time-to-first-update expectations, use of internal signals (error/latency thresholds) to drive component status, and the review/approval guardrails for high severity incidents. Northbridge requested examples of publishable post-incident summaries and clarification on notification methods (email/RSS/webhook) and retention of incident history.
topics: Incident declaration: severity levels, criteria, and customer notification triggers
Status page components: granularity by product surface and region
Post-incident summaries: content, timing, confidentiality boundaries
Dedicated/Private comms: visibility constraints and customer-specific incidents
Customer escalation path when status accuracy is disputed
next_steps: Redwood (Naomi) to send SOC 2 summary + incident communications overview (roles, approval flow, and sample templates).
Redwood (Kira) to share 2 example post-incident summaries (redacted) and link to public status page incident history.
Northbridge (Samantha) to confirm whether they require webhook delivery for incident updates vs email/RSS.
Schedule a 30-min follow-up with Northbridge platform team to review Dedicated vs Hosted incident visibility expectations.
action_items: Redwood/Naomi: Provide written explanation of incident declaration criteria (Sev0-Sev3) and time-to-first-update target ranges by severity.
Redwood/Kira: Send status page component list and how it maps to product surfaces (Hosted API, Streaming, Embeddings, Reranking, Console) and regions.
Redwood/Michael: Confirm what legal review is required for publishable post-incident summaries and the boundaries on sharing RCAs.
Northbridge/Samantha: List any contractual requirements for incident notification SLAs and post-incident report timelines.
Northbridge/Megan: Share security questionnaire section(s) related to incident communications and approval requirements.
questions: How do you decide when to declare an incident vs treat it as an internal degradation?
Who is allowed to post to the status page and do updates require approval?
What do you include in post-incident summaries (root cause, affected customers, regions, metrics)?
How do you handle incidents that only affect a single dedicated tenant or private deployment?
Do you publish latency-only degradations or only error-based outages?
How can customers dispute status accuracy and what evidence do you provide?
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Date: 2025-11-20
Time: 9:00 AM PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Call type: Security review

Attendees
- Redwood Inference: Kira Thompson, Naomi Feldman, Michael Grant, Dev Patel
- Northbridge AI Platform: Samantha Reed, Arjun Patel, Megan O'Connor, Lena Cho

---

[00:00] Kira Thompson: Alright, I think we’re recording. Thanks everyone for making time. This is the security review, focused on incident process and the status page, right?

[00:10] Samantha Reed: Yep. Specifically incident declaration, comms approvals, and post-incident summaries. We’ve had pain with vendors where the status page is… vague.

[00:21] Kira Thompson: Got it. Naomi and Michael are on as well. Naomi covers security/compliance, Michael helps on what we can publish and how we phrase it.

[00:30] Naomi Feldman: Hi everyone.

[00:31] Michael Grant: Hello.

[00:33] Megan O'Connor: And I’m Megan from procurement. I may ask about contractual language.

[00:38] Kira Thompson: Perfect.

[00:41] Arjun Patel: I’m Arjun, platform eng. I’ll probably ask about what signals actually drive the status page.

[00:47] Kira Thompson: Great.

[00:50] Kira Thompson: Maybe Samantha, do you want to start with your top questions so we can go point by point?

[01:00] Samantha Reed: Sure. One: how do you decide it’s an incident, like who declares it and what criteria. Two: who can update the status page and is there an approval step. Three: what info do you publish after, like postmortems, summaries, that kind of thing.

[01:19] Kira Thompson: Makes sense. I’ll start with the process and then we can go deeper.

[01:24] Kira Thompson: Internally we run an incident process with defined roles: Incident Commander, Comms Lead, and Scribe. The IC is accountable for mitigation and coordination. Comms Lead owns customer-facing updates: status page and coordination with Support. Scribe captures timeline notes.

[01:45] Lena Cho: Is that 24/7? Like is Comms Lead always staffed?

[01:49] Kira Thompson: We have on-call coverage 24/7 for incident response. Comms Lead is assigned as part of the incident workflow when severity hits a threshold. In lower severity, it can be the IC or on-call, but in high severity we explicitly assign it.

[02:06] Samantha Reed: Okay. And declaration criteria?

[02:10] Naomi Feldman: We use severity levels, roughly Sev0 through Sev3. Sev0 is broad outage or critical customer impact, Sev1 is significant degradation or partial outage with material impact, Sev2 is limited scope or short-lived, Sev3 is mostly informational.

[02:26] Naomi Feldman: Criteria is based on observed customer impact signals: elevated error rates, latency beyond SLO thresholds, inability to authenticate, things like that. We try not to declare incidents purely on “one dashboard is red” if it’s internal-only.

[02:43] Arjun Patel: When you say SLO thresholds—are those per region? per endpoint?

[02:47] Kira Thompson: For hosted services, yes, we track per region and per capability where it matters—like streaming can degrade differently than non-streaming.

[02:56] Arjun Patel: That’s exactly what we’ve seen. Streaming disconnects but the rest is fine.

[03:00] Kira Thompson: Right. And to your point, we’ve been improving component granularity on the status page to reflect that. Historically vendors have “API” as one thing, but we split by product surface and region.

[03:12] Samantha Reed: So you’d show “Streaming - US East” as degraded but not “Embeddings - EU”?

[03:17] Kira Thompson: Yes, that’s the goal and what we’re implementing.

[03:22] Megan O'Connor: Is it live today or in progress?

[03:24] Kira Thompson: Some of it is live, and additional granularity is in rollout. We can show you the component taxonomy we’re converging on.

[03:34] Samantha Reed: For our review, we just need to know what’s the commitment and process, not necessarily exact UI.

[03:41] Kira Thompson: Understood.

[03:44] Samantha Reed: On approvals: who can post? We require change control for external communications in some cases.

[03:52] Naomi Feldman: Practically, status page updates are performed by the Comms Lead or the IC through our incident tooling. For Sev0/Sev1 we have an approval guardrail—meaning a second set of eyes. Usually IC or Support lead, depending.

[04:08] Dev Patel: Yeah, from Support side, for the biggest events we want alignment so the status page and what our agents say match. Otherwise tickets explode.

[04:18] Samantha Reed: Is that an actual workflow step or informal?

[04:21] Naomi Feldman: It’s workflow-backed. Not every update needs legal, but for high severity we require an internal approval before publishing certain language, especially anything that could imply SLA breach, customer-specific info, or security incidents.

[04:38] Michael Grant: And just to be clear, most updates are operational and time-sensitive. We don’t bottleneck them through legal review in the moment. The guardrail is about accuracy and sensitive content, not slowing updates.

[04:53] Lena Cho: What about security incidents specifically? Like a suspected breach.

[04:57] Naomi Feldman: Those are handled under our security incident response process with separate notification requirements. We do not post suspected security incidents on the public status page as “degraded API” if it’s actually a security containment event. We handle customer notifications directly as appropriate.

[05:15] Samantha Reed: Okay, that’s good.

[05:17] Arjun Patel: On time to first update, do you have targets? Like 15 minutes? 30 minutes?

[05:23] Kira Thompson: We track time-to-first-update. For Sev0/Sev1 we aim to post an initial update quickly once we’ve confirmed impact and component scope. I don’t want to promise a number on a call, but we can share typical ranges and our process.

[05:39] Megan O'Connor: We might need a range for procurement. Not a hard SLA but an expectation.

[05:44] Michael Grant: We can provide “target” language rather than contractual SLA, unless we negotiate it. Many customers accept a target like “as soon as practical, typically within X.”

[05:56] Samantha Reed: That’s fine. We want consistency more than a perfect number.

[06:03] Kira Thompson: Totally.

[06:06] Arjun Patel: Can we talk about what “confirmed impact” means? Like, are you waiting for internal burn rate or something?

[06:12] Kira Thompson: It’s a mix. We look at error rate, latency percentiles, and streaming disconnect metrics. We have anti-flap logic to avoid toggling a component based on transient spikes.

[06:25] Arjun Patel: Anti flap. Like hysteresis windows.

[06:27] Kira Thompson: Exactly.

[06:30] Samantha Reed: But doesn’t that delay the status page?

[06:33] Naomi Feldman: It can, but we balance it. The goal is to avoid whiplash—marking degraded for 2 minutes and then back to operational. For severe impact we still update quickly; anti-flap mainly affects automated signals and the “recovered” transition.

[06:53] Dev Patel: From Support, the worst is “it says resolved” and then it’s not. So we’re careful with the resolved state.

[07:02] Samantha Reed: That makes sense.

[07:04] Kira Thompson: Also, initial updates can be “Investigating” with partial information. We’ll say what we know: e.g., “We’re investigating elevated errors on Streaming in us-east; other regions appear unaffected.”

[07:20] Samantha Reed: Do you commit to include region and component in the first update?

[07:23] Kira Thompson: That’s the standard we’re moving to, yes.

[07:29] Megan O'Connor: Can you share the exact template language you use?

[07:32] Kira Thompson: We can share the template categories and example text. Some internal bits are not shared, but the public-facing phrasing we can provide.

[07:42] Michael Grant: The template is designed to be publishable without accidentally disclosing sensitive details like a specific customer workload or capacity constraints.

[07:52] Samantha Reed: That’s actually my next question: post-incident summaries. What’s included?

[07:57] Kira Thompson: We publish a post-incident summary after resolution for significant incidents. It includes a high-level impact statement (what was affected), time window, what we did to mitigate, and prevention steps. We avoid customer names, request payload content, and anything that could expose infrastructure weaknesses.

[08:17] Lena Cho: Do you include root cause?

[08:20] Kira Thompson: We include a root cause *class* and a description at an appropriate level. Example: “a configuration change to the gateway routing layer caused elevated 5xx in us-east,” or “a downstream dependency led to increased timeouts.” We typically do not include exploit-level detail.

[08:41] Michael Grant: Right, we aim for transparency without providing a playbook for abuse, and without disclosing proprietary details.

[08:48] Samantha Reed: Understood. Do you share full postmortems privately?

[08:52] Kira Thompson: For enterprise customers, we can share more detailed reports under NDA depending on the incident and the scope. But the default public artifact is the summary.

[09:03] Arjun Patel: Do you list affected endpoints? Like /v1/embeddings vs chat completions.

[09:08] Kira Thompson: Often yes, at the level of “Embeddings API” or “Streaming responses.” We may also mention “subset of routes” if it’s narrow.

[09:19] Samantha Reed: Approval for post-incident summary: who signs off?

[09:22] Naomi Feldman: Typically the IC and Comms Lead, and for certain cases, Security or Legal. But we aim to publish quickly and not spend weeks.

[09:33] Megan O'Connor: Timing expectation? Like within five business days.

[09:36] Kira Thompson: We can align on expectations. Common is within a week for larger incidents. For smaller, sometimes same day. We’ll follow up with policy language.

[09:47] Samantha Reed: Great.

[09:49] Arjun Patel: Dedicated and private: what happens if only our dedicated pool is impacted? Do you post that publicly?

[09:56] Kira Thompson: Good question. For Dedicated, we generally do not mark the entire public status page as degraded if only a single tenant is impacted, because that would be misleading and could leak customer-specific issues. We handle tenant-specific comms directly.

[10:14] Samantha Reed: So we would get a direct notification?

[10:16] Dev Patel: Yes, Support/CS will contact you through agreed channels if it’s your environment.

[10:22] Lena Cho: For private deployments, same?

[10:24] Kira Thompson: Same idea. Private deployments can have different networking and customer-managed parts. Public status page focuses on shared services; private is handled through support channels.

[10:38] Arjun Patel: That’s fine as long as it’s clear in the contract. We’ve had vendors hide behind “private, so no status.”

[10:45] Kira Thompson: Totally. We want clarity.

[10:49] Samantha Reed: On the status page itself—do you have region breakdown today? We care about us-east and eu-west separately.

[10:56] Kira Thompson: Yes, we can provide region breakdown for major regions. Again, we’re increasing component granularity. The direction is product surface x region.

[11:09] Arjun Patel: What about failure modes? Like auth vs inference.

[11:12] Kira Thompson: In some cases, we separate capability components (e.g., “Authentication” vs “Inference API”). But we try not to over-fragment because it becomes confusing.

[11:25] Samantha Reed: Makes sense.

[11:27] Megan O'Connor: Notification methods: can we subscribe via email? Do you support webhooks?

[11:33] Kira Thompson: Email and RSS are typical. Webhooks depend on provider capability; we can discuss options. Many customers consume RSS into Slack.

[11:46] Arjun Patel: We’d like a webhook or at least Atom feed.

[11:49] Kira Thompson: Noted.

[11:52] Samantha Reed: Back to approvals: you said second set of eyes for Sev0/Sev1. Who is that? Is it always Support?

[12:00] Dev Patel: Not always. Often it’s IC approves and Comms Lead posts, or Comms Lead drafts and IC approves. Support is looped in for major customer-facing impact.

[12:13] Naomi Feldman: And for language touching security or compliance, we escalate to Security and/or Legal.

[12:20] Samantha Reed: Does that slow updates?

[12:22] Michael Grant: Generally no, because early updates don’t include sensitive details. If there’s a question like “should we state that a vendor was at fault,” we might advise more conservative language.

[12:38] Samantha Reed: Okay.

[12:40] Arjun Patel: Do you ever auto-update the status page based on metrics?

[12:44] Kira Thompson: We’re cautious there. Some signals can suggest component impact, but humans control public updates today. We do automate drafting and reminders—so the Comms Lead gets suggested text and the right components pre-selected.

[13:03] Arjun Patel: That’s good. Automated toggling can be scary.

[13:06] Kira Thompson: Yeah.

[13:08] Samantha Reed: Can you walk us through a concrete scenario? Say elevated 500s on embeddings in us-east.

[13:15] Kira Thompson: Sure. On detection, on-call confirms via dashboards that embeddings requests are failing above threshold. IC opens an incident and assigns roles. Comms Lead posts an “Investigating” update: “We’re investigating elevated error rates for Embeddings API in US-East; other APIs/regions appear normal.”

[13:37] Kira Thompson: As we identify cause, we update to “Identified” and include mitigation steps like “we’re rolling back a config change” or “shifting traffic.” Once metrics stabilize, we move to “Monitoring” and then “Resolved.”

[13:55] Samantha Reed: And the post-incident summary later?

[13:58] Kira Thompson: Includes the window, impact magnitude in general terms, what we changed, and follow-ups.

[14:08] Lena Cho: Do you share exact error percentages?

[14:10] Kira Thompson: Sometimes ranges or qualitative descriptions. Exact numbers can be tricky and sometimes misleading depending on sample. But we can include “elevated errors” plus duration.

[14:24] Arjun Patel: For us, even a rough magnitude helps. Like “up to 20% of requests failed.”

[14:29] Kira Thompson: We hear that. We can incorporate a magnitude where it’s safe and accurate.

[14:37] Samantha Reed: How do you ensure you don’t leak customer-specific info?

[14:41] Michael Grant: Our templates explicitly prohibit mentioning specific customers, tenant identifiers, unique workloads, or “we ran out of capacity for customer X.” We also avoid sharing precise capacity numbers.

[14:57] Naomi Feldman: We also have audit logs internally of who posted what and when. That helps with governance.

[15:04] Lena Cho: Audit logs for status page posts?

[15:06] Naomi Feldman: Yes, internally. It’s not a public feed, but it exists for compliance.

[15:13] Samantha Reed: That’s helpful.

[15:15] Megan O'Connor: Another procurement question: if the status page is wrong, what’s the escalation?

[15:21] Dev Patel: Customers can open a support ticket or contact their CSM. We have an escalation path to SRE leadership for status accuracy disputes, and we’ll share evidence like timestamps and relevant dashboard snapshots when appropriate.

[15:39] Samantha Reed: Okay.

[15:41] Arjun Patel: You mentioned dashboards. Is there a customer-facing view or just internal?

[15:45] Kira Thompson: Primarily internal. We may share certain views during an incident, but we don’t expose raw internal telemetry publicly.

[15:55] Samantha Reed: That’s fine.

[15:58] Kira Thompson: Anything else on incident declaration?

[16:02] Samantha Reed: Are there circumstances you *won’t* declare an incident publicly even if there’s customer impact?

[16:09] Naomi Feldman: If it’s isolated to a single dedicated tenant, we generally won’t mark a broad public component. We will notify impacted customers directly. If it’s a security containment, we follow security incident process and direct notifications.

[16:24] Samantha Reed: Understood.

[16:26] Megan O'Connor: Does the contract differentiate those cases? Like hosted vs dedicated.

[16:30] Michael Grant: We can document it. Hosted status page is appropriate for shared services. Dedicated/private communications are typically direct per customer. We can add language to avoid ambiguity.

[16:47] Lena Cho: Can you commit to a post-incident report timeframe for dedicated incidents too?

[16:52] Kira Thompson: We can discuss. Typically yes for significant incidents, but the artifact may be shared privately rather than posted publicly.

[17:02] Samantha Reed: Great.

[17:04] Arjun Patel: Another point: do you mark “degraded performance” for latency increases even without errors?

[17:10] Kira Thompson: Yes, if latency crosses a threshold and impacts customer experience materially. It’s not only 5xx.

[17:20] Arjun Patel: Good.

[17:22] Samantha Reed: But again you avoid flapping.

[17:24] Kira Thompson: Correct.

[17:26] Megan O'Connor: For notification, do you notify customers proactively or do they need to check status page?

[17:33] Dev Patel: For major incidents we push notifications via the status page subscription mechanism. For tenant-specific we contact you via your agreed channel.

[17:44] Samantha Reed: Okay.

[17:46] Kira Thompson: We’re almost halfway. Do you want to dive into post-incident summary content in more detail?

[17:52] Samantha Reed: Yes. Specifically: do you include timelines, like “09:12 detected, 09:20 mitigated.”

[17:58] Kira Thompson: Yes, a simplified timeline is common. Not every internal event, but key milestones.

[18:07] Lena Cho: And follow-ups? Like prevention items.

[18:10] Kira Thompson: Yes, we list preventive actions. Sometimes “completed,” “in progress,” etc. We try to make it actionable.

[18:20] Michael Grant: We may generalize the language, like “improved monitoring and rollback safeguards,” rather than “we changed this exact firewall rule,” depending.

[18:33] Arjun Patel: Do you link to an external postmortem doc?

[18:36] Kira Thompson: Typically the summary is on the incident page and may include a link if there’s a more detailed public write-up. Often it’s just the summary.

[18:49] Samantha Reed: Okay.

[18:51] Megan O'Connor: We’re going to need examples to show our risk committee.

[18:55] Kira Thompson: We can provide redacted examples.

[18:58] Naomi Feldman: Yes.

[19:01] Samantha Reed: Last thing: what’s your process if you discover the initial status update was wrong? Like wrong region.

[19:08] Kira Thompson: We correct it and we note the correction in the incident updates. Internally we also do an accuracy review to reduce recurrence.

[19:20] Dev Patel: And we align with Support macros so we don’t contradict ourselves.

[19:26] Samantha Reed: Great.

[19:29] Arjun Patel: Do you have a “partial outage” vs “degraded performance” taxonomy?

[19:33] Kira Thompson: Yes. It’s generally aligned to error rate severity and customer impact. Again, we can share how we define those states.

[19:45] Samantha Reed: Please do.

[19:47] Kira Thompson: Noted.

[19:50] (crosstalk)

[19:51] Megan O'Connor: Sorry, one more. Is there any approval from customer success required to post?

[19:56] Dev Patel: Not required, but we often coordinate. For Sev0/Sev1 there is an approval step—think IC or Support lead—not “CS leadership.”

[20:07] Megan O'Connor: Got it.

[20:10] Kira Thompson: We can talk about channels. If you want a named distribution list on your side for dedicated notifications, we can do that.

[20:19] Samantha Reed: Yes, we’ll provide that.

[20:22] Kira Thompson: Great.

[20:24] Arjun Patel: What about maintenance windows? Do you post planned maintenance?

[20:28] Kira Thompson: Yes, we post scheduled maintenance and planned degradations when relevant.

[20:35] Samantha Reed: Okay.

[20:37] Naomi Feldman: Also, for compliance, we retain incident records and status updates. If you need retention details, we can provide.

[20:46] Lena Cho: Please include retention of incident history visible publicly.

[20:50] Kira Thompson: Sure.

[20:52] Samantha Reed: I think that covers it.

[20:54] Kira Thompson: Great. I’ll recap next steps at the end.

[21:00] Kira Thompson: Any final questions before we switch to Q&A style?

[21:05] Samantha Reed: Maybe just clarify the “second set of eyes” again. Is it mandatory?

[21:10] Naomi Feldman: For Sev0/Sev1, yes for initial post and for any update that changes the scope materially or includes cause/mitigation claims. For lower severity, it’s not mandatory.

[21:25] Samantha Reed: Great.

[21:28] Arjun Patel: If the Comms Lead is out, who does it?

[21:31] Kira Thompson: IC can do it, and our tooling will prompt. We also have reminders in the incident channel.

[21:40] Arjun Patel: Cool.

[21:42] Megan O'Connor: Do you have a dedicated security contact or mailbox for incident notifications?

[21:47] Naomi Feldman: Yes, we can provide a security contact channel for security-specific notifications.

[21:54] Megan O'Connor: Good.

[21:56] Kira Thompson: Alright, last 10 minutes: I’ll list what we’ll send.

[22:02] Kira Thompson: Naomi will send a short write-up of incident declaration criteria and roles/approval flow, plus SOC2 summary material. I’ll send examples of post-incident summaries and a link to incident history and component definitions.

[22:20] Kira Thompson: Northbridge, you’ll confirm whether webhook vs RSS is required and send any contractual notification requirements.

[22:29] Samantha Reed: Yep.

[22:30] Megan O'Connor: And I’ll send the questionnaire sections.

[22:33] Kira Thompson: Great.

[22:35] Michael Grant: If there’s any redline language about notification timing, loop me in.

[22:41] Megan O'Connor: Will do.

[22:43] Kira Thompson: Thanks all.

[22:46] (meeting continues with brief scheduling and wrap)

[51:40] Kira Thompson: Okay, we’ll stop recording. Thanks.

---
End of transcript
